reason: E1 directly supports impurity-induced phase segregation and softening during 700°C aging in a Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy, but it does not report nanoscale brittle precipitates, PFZs, or toughness reduction under mechanical loading. E2 reports brittleness in a different RHEA after HIP, but attributes it to an HCP phase from processing, not trace impurities, and does not support the specific mechanism or controlled comparison. Thus, only the general premise of impurity-driven segregation is partially supported, while the specific microstructural features, toughness loss, and loading conditions lack direct
premises: Trace interstitial impurities (O, N) in RHEAs promote phase segregation during thermal aging at 700°C
Impurity-driven segregation leads to nanoscale brittle precipitates or PFZs near grain boundaries
These features impede dislocation mobility and promote crack initiation, reducing toughness
The effect is measurable as a 20–30% reduction in fracture toughness under service-like loading
The mechanism is activated at service temperatures where diffusion occurs but below full homogenization
